knowledgeNodes.name: Cover Letter Header and Contact Information
knowledgeNodes.nameEn: Cover Letter Header and Contact Information
knowledgeNodes.definition: Header sequence: applicant full name, street address, phone number, professional email, full written date, hiring manager name/title/company/address. Professional email should use applicant's legal name, avoid numeric addresses.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.

knowledgeNodes.name: Cover Letter Salutation and Opening Paragraph
knowledgeNodes.nameEn: Cover Letter Salutation and Opening Paragraph

knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.

knowledgeNodes.name: Cover Letter Closing and Sign-Off
knowledgeNodes.definition: Closing paragraph: thank the hiring manager and include a confident call to action for an interview. Sign-off: 'Sincerely,' followed by typed full name; optional digital signature.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.

options.label: A
options.text: To list all of your work and education history in paragraph form.
options.feedbackWrong: That is the purpose of a resume, not a cover letter. A cover letter tells a targeted story.

options.label: B
options.text: To introduce yourself and request an interview politely.
options.feedbackWrong: While polite, this is too vague. A cover letter specifically connects your skills to the employer's needs.

options.label: C
options.text: To connect your skills and experiences to the specific employer's needs in a professional story.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! A cover letter is a narrative that shows why you are a great fit for the job.

options.label: D
options.text: To show off your vocabulary and writing style.
options.feedbackWrong: Writing style matters, but the core purpose is to match your skills to the job, not to impress with language.

questions.stemIntent: Check if student knows to avoid 'To Whom It May Concern' or 'Hello' and use a role-based salutation.

options.label: A
options.text: To Whom It May Concern,
options.feedbackWrong: Too generic. Try to address the specific role or department.

options.label: B
options.text: Hello,
options.feedbackWrong: Too casual for a formal cover letter. Always use a professional salutation.

options.label: C
options.text: Dear Sir/Madam,
options.feedbackWrong: Outdated and generic. Use a more specific alternative.

options.label: D
options.text: To the Retail Manager Hiring Team at SportChek,
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! This salutation is specific and professional.

questions.stem: Which sentence from a cover letter opening paragraph would be most effective?
questions.successCriteria: Student identifies that the opening must state the job title and enthusiasm, not ask a question.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces ...
questions.alignmentNote: Question focuses on the opening paragraph of a cover letter, a key component of this form.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student avoids opening with a question and instead states the job and enthusiasm.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think opening with 'Are you hiring?' is acceptable.

options.label: A
options.text: Are you looking for a hardworking employee?
options.feedbackWrong: Never open with a question. It signals you haven't researched the company.

options.label: B
options.text: I am writing to apply for the Sales Associate position at your downtown location, and I am excited about the opportunity to contribute to your team.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! This sentence states the exact job and shows genuine enthusiasm.

options.label: C
options.text: I think I would be great for this job because I have experience.
options.feedbackWrong: Too vague. Specify the job title and show enthusiasm.

options.label: D
options.text: You probably receive many applications, but mine is special.
options.feedbackWrong: Unprofessional. Focus on the job and your fit.

questions.stem: What should the closing paragraph of a cover letter include?
questions.successCriteria: Student knows that a confident call to action for an interview is required.
questions.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces ...
questions.alignmentNote: Closing paragraph conventions are part of the cover letter form under B2.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student recalls the call-to-action requirement.
questions.commonMisconception: Students think only thanking is sufficient, or they omit the interview request.

options.label: A
options.text: Only a thank-you and hope to hear from you.
options.feedbackWrong: A thank-you is good, but you also need a confident call to action requesting an interview.

options.label: B
options.text: A thank-you, a statement of my availability, and a clear request for an interview (e.g., 'I look forward to discussing my qualifications further in an interview.').
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! The closing should thank and confidently request an interview.

options.label: C
options.text: A list of all my skills again.
options.feedbackWrong: The closing is not for repeating skills; it's for a call to action.

options.label: D
options.text: A question about the hiring timeline.
options.feedbackWrong: Avoid questions in the closing. State your request for an interview.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects an option equating cover letter to a resume or simple introduction.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks a cover letter is merely a restatement of the resume or a polite introduction, rather than a targeted narrative that connects their skills to the employer's specific needs.

miniLesson.explain: A cover letter is a professional story that connects your skills and experiences to the employer's needs. Unlike a resume which lists facts, a cover letter shows why you are a good fit and demonstrates enthusiasm for the specific job. For example, Sam Foster's letter connected his school fundraiser cash handling to retail skills and his basketball experience to an athletic footwear company.
miniLesson.example: Low-quality: Deirdre's letter with missing info, casual greeting, and irrelevant hobbies. High-quality: Sam Foster's letter with proper header, experience translation, and enthusiasm.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Cover = Connect: Your letter must connect your story to their needs.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following is the main purpose of a cover letter? A) To list all your experience in paragraph form B) To tell a story that links your skills to the employer's needs C) To introduce yourself formally D) To ask for an interview
guidedPractice.answer: B) To tell a story that links your skills to the employer's needs.

guidedPractice.prompt: A student is applying for a cashier job. Which excerpt would be best in the cover letter? A) 'I worked at a grocery store for one year.' B) 'My year as a grocery store cashier taught me to handle money accurately and provide friendly customer service, skills I can use at your store.' C) 'I am a hard worker and dedicated employee.' D) 'I have experience in retail.' Explain why.
guidedPractice.answer: B) because it connects the experience to specific skills (cash handling, customer service) relevant to the job.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the following opening from a cover letter: 'I am applying for the job at your company. I have worked many jobs and I think I would be a good fit.' Rewrite it to follow cover letter purpose rules. Provide your rewrite.
guidedPractice.answer: I am excited to apply for the Sales Associate position at SportChek. My experience as a team captain has developed my leadership and communication skills, and my school fundraiser taught me cash handling and customer service, which I am eager to bring to your team.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q2 that uses 'Hello' or 'To Whom It May Concern'
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may use casual greetings like 'Hello' or generic 'To Whom It May Concern' instead of a specific salutation.

miniLesson.explain: A cover letter salutation must be specific and professional. Avoid casual greetings like 'Hello' or generic phrases like 'To Whom It May Concern'. Instead, address the hiring manager directly if you know their name, or use 'To the [Role] Hiring Manager at [Company]' if the name is unknown. This shows you have researched the company and are taking the application seriously.
miniLesson.example:
Wrong: 'Hello,'
Wrong: 'To Whom It May Concern,'
Correct: 'To the Retail Manager Hiring Team at SportChek,'
Correct: 'Dear Ms. Johnson,'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Avoid 'Hello', use 'To the [Role]'. Be specific, not generic.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which salutation is most appropriate for a cover letter when you do not know the hiring manager's name?
guidedPractice.answer: To the Retail Manager Hiring Team at SportChek,

guidedPractice.prompt: You are applying for a Sales Associate position at Best Buy. You do not know the hiring manager's name. Write an appropriate salutation.
guidedPractice.answer: To the Sales Associate Hiring Manager at Best Buy,

guidedPractice.prompt: A student wrote: 'Hello, I am applying for the job.' Revise the greeting to be professional and specific. Assume the company is 'ABC Corp' and the role is 'Marketing Intern'.
guidedPractice.answer: To the Marketing Intern Hiring Manager at ABC Corp,

reteachModules.trigger: Student chooses an opening that begins with a question like 'Are you hiring?' or fails to state the exact job title and enthusiasm.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think it's acceptable to open with a question like 'Are you hiring?' as a way to engage the reader, not realizing it signals a lack of research and unprofessionalism.

miniLesson.explain: The opening paragraph of a cover letter must immediately state the exact job title and express genuine enthusiasm for the role. Never open with a question such as 'Are you hiring?' because it shows you haven't researched the company and it sounds unprofessional.
miniLesson.example: Instead of 'Are you looking for a hardworking employee?', write 'I am excited to apply for the Sales Associate position at your downtown location, and I am confident my customer service experience makes me a great fit.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Don't ask, state! Jump right into the job title and your excitement.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following is a correct opening sentence for a cover letter? A) 'Are you hiring? I have great skills.' B) 'I am writing to apply for the Retail Sales position at your Queen St. store, and I am eager to bring my teamwork abilities to your team.' C) 'Hello, I would like a job.'
guidedPractice.answer: B) 'I am writing to apply for the Retail Sales position at your Queen St. store, and I am eager to bring my teamwork abilities to your team.'

guidedPractice.prompt: Revise the following opening to make it effective: 'Are you hiring? I think I could help your store.'
guidedPractice.answer: I am writing to apply for the Sales Associate position at your store, and I am excited about the opportunity to contribute to your team with my strong customer service skills.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a complete opening sentence for a cover letter applying to the position of Customer Service Representative at Best Buy. Include the exact job title and show genuine enthusiasm.
guidedPractice.answer: I am thrilled to apply for the Customer Service Representative position at Best Buy, and I am eager to use my problem-solving and communication skills to help customers find the best technology solutions.

reteachModules.trigger: Student's cover letter closing paragraph omits a call to action for an interview, only including a thank-you.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think that simply thanking the employer and expressing hope to hear from them is sufficient, forgetting to explicitly and confidently request an interview.

miniLesson.explain: The closing paragraph of a cover letter must do two things: thank the hiring manager for their time and include a confident call to action requesting an interview. A call to action shows initiative and interest, e.g., 'I look forward to discussing my qualifications further in an interview.' Without it, the letter feels incomplete and passive.
miniLesson.example: Weak: 'Thank you for your time. I hope to hear from you soon.' Strong: 'Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how my skills align with your team's needs in an interview.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Close with confidence: thank AND ask for the interview.

guidedPractice.prompt: Fill in the blanks to complete a proper closing paragraph: 'Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss my qualifications further in an _______.'
guidedPractice.answer: interview

guidedPractice.prompt: Which closing paragraph is more effective? A: 'Thank you for reading my letter. I hope you call me.' B: 'Thank you for your time. I am eager to discuss how my experience can benefit your team in an interview.' Explain why.
guidedPractice.answer: B is more effective because it thanks the employer and includes a confident call to action for an interview, showing professionalism and initiative. Option A is too passive and lacks a direct request.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write a closing paragraph for a cover letter applying for a retail sales associate position. Include a thank-you and a confident call to action for an interview.
guidedPractice.answer: Thank you for considering my application. I am excited about the opportunity to bring my customer service and cash handling skills to your team and would welcome the chance to discuss my qualifications in an interview.

reteachModules.trigger: You included all your experiences in the cover letter without connecting them to the job.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often list their resume experiences in paragraph form without linking them to the employer's needs, making the cover letter a repetitive summary rather than a targeted story.

miniLesson.explain: A cover letter is not a duplicate of your resume. It is a focused narrative that connects your specific skills and experiences to the requirements of the job. For each experience, explain how it prepared you for the role you're applying for.
miniLesson.example: For a retail position, instead of saying 'I was team captain of basketball', say: 'As basketball team captain, I developed leadership and communication skills by coordinating schedules and motivating teammates, which I can use to assist customers and support store operations.'
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: S.T.O.R.Y. - Skills That Open the Role's Yonder: Translate each experience into a skill the job needs.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which sentence connects experience to job? A: 'I worked at a bake sale.' B: 'I managed cash and customer service at a bake sale, skills needed for retail.'
guidedPractice.answer: B

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite this resume-style sentence to connect to a retail job: 'I was treasurer of the student council.'
guidedPractice.answer: As student council treasurer, I handled budgets and transactions, building the cash management skills essential for a retail associate.

guidedPractice.prompt: You are applying for a customer service role. Write a short paragraph linking your experience as a library volunteer to the job.
guidedPractice.answer: Volunteering at the library taught me to assist patrons with inquiries, organize materials, and maintain a welcoming environment, directly preparing me to provide excellent customer service in your store.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects Microsoft Word (.docx) as the correct file format in the diagnostic.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student thinks Word format is acceptable and does not recognize that PDF is required to preserve formatting.

miniLesson.explain: Employers require cover letters in PDF format because PDFs keep your layout, fonts, and spacing exactly as you designed them. Word documents can shift formatting when opened on different computers or operating systems, potentially making your letter look unprofessional. Always convert your final cover letter to PDF before submitting.
miniLesson.example: Compare: A Word document with a table might display incorrectly on a hiring manager's screen, while the same file saved as PDF remains perfect. Also, PDFs cannot be accidentally edited, ensuring your work stays original.

guidedPractice.prompt: What file format should you use when submitting your cover letter to an employer?
guidedPractice.answer: PDF (.pdf)

guidedPractice.prompt: A student saves their cover letter as 'CoverLetter.docx' and submits it. Why is this a problem?
guidedPractice.answer: The .docx format can cause formatting issues on the employer's computer, and Word documents are editable, which is unprofessional. The correct format is PDF.

guidedPractice.prompt: The job posting says 'Submit your cover letter as a PDF attachment.' Your friend says they always use Word because it's easier to edit. What should you say to your friend?
guidedPractice.answer: I would explain that the employer specifically requested PDF to ensure consistent formatting and professionalism. Even though Word is easier to edit, it's important to follow the instructions and save the final version as a PDF before submitting.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q7 that has missing or incorrect header info
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may omit or incorrectly order header information, such as forgetting the phone number or using numeric dates.

miniLesson.explain: The header of a cover letter must include your full name, street address, phone number, professional email, the full written date (e.g., June 5, 2026), and the hiring manager's name, title, company, and address. Each element is required and must appear in this order. A missing phone number or address prevents employers from contacting you.
miniLesson.example:
Jordan Lee
123 Maple Street, Toronto, Ontario M5V 2T6
(416) 555-0198
jordan.lee@email.com
June 5, 2026
Ms. Sarah Chen, Hiring Manager
ABC Company
456 King Street West, Toronto, Ontario M5V 1K4
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Name, Address, Phone, Email, Date, Manager, Company (NAP-EMC)

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which required piece of information is missing from this header?

Sam Foster
42 Oak Avenue, Ottawa, Ontario K1A 0B1
sam.foster@email.com
July 15, 2026
Hiring Manager
SportChek

reteachModules.trigger: Student includes personal hobbies that do not connect to the target role.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think any personal interest can be included in a cover letter, but only experiences that can be translated into workplace skills relevant to the job should be included.

miniLesson.explain: Cover letters should only include experiences that can be connected to the job's requirements. Irrelevant hobbies like video gaming, unless directly relevant, weaken your application. Focus on transferable skills from school, clubs, or volunteer work.
miniLesson.example: Bad: 'I enjoy playing video games.' (no connection to retail). Good: 'Organizing a school bake sale helped me develop cash handling and customer service skills.' (directly relevant).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Ask yourself: 'Does this help me do the job?' Only include if yes.

guidedPractice.prompt:
Which of the following would be a good experience to include in a cover letter for a retail job?
A) I like to play soccer.
B) I managed the school store.
C) I watch TV.
D) I do yoga.
guidedPractice.answer: B) I managed the school store.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rewrite the following sentence to make it relevant to a retail job: 'I was a member of the debate club.'
guidedPractice.answer: As a member of the debate club, I developed strong communication and persuasion skills, which will help me assist customers and handle complaints.

guidedPractice.prompt:
For a summer internship at a marketing firm, which extracurricular experience should you highlight?
A) Being the captain of the chess team.
B) Playing guitar in a band.
C) Volunteering to create social media posts for a local charity.
D) Attending art classes.
guidedPractice.answer: C) Volunteering to create social media posts for a local charity, because it directly relates to marketing and content creation skills.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the purpose of a cover letter?
options: To list all your work experience in paragraph form.
To tell a story that connects your skills to the employer's needs.
To provide a formal introduction and request an interview.
To repeat the information on your resume in a different format.

questions.stem: You are applying for a summer job at a local bookstore. Describe one experience from school or extracurriculars that you could include in your cover letter, and explain how you would translate it to show the employer you are a good fit.
questions.rubric: The response must include: (1) a specific experience from school or extracurriculars, (2) a clear translation of that experience into a relevant skill (e.g., organization, customer service, teamwork), and (3) a connection to the bookstore job (e.g., organizing books, helping customers, working with a team).

retestCards.passRule: Q1 must select option 2. Q2 must include a specific experience, a clear translation into a relevant skill, and a connection to the bookstore job. Both questions must be correct to pass.

questions.stem: Which salutation is most appropriate for a cover letter when you do not know the hiring manager's name?
options: Hello,
To Whom It May Concern,
To the Sales Associate Hiring Manager at Best Buy,
Dear Hiring Manager,

questions.stem: You are applying for a Marketing Intern position at ABC Corp. You do not know the hiring manager's name. Write an appropriate salutation for your cover letter.
questions.rubric: The salutation must be specific to the role and company, using the format 'To the [Role] Hiring Manager at [Company],' or similar. Avoid casual greetings like 'Hello' or generic 'To Whom It May Concern'. Accept 'To the Marketing Intern Hiring Manager at ABC Corp,' or 'To the Marketing Intern Hiring Team at ABC Corp,' etc.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct option (index 2) and provide a salutation that is specific to the role and company, without using 'Hello' or 'To Whom It May Concern'.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an appropriate opening for a cover letter for a Sales Associate position at SportChek?
options: Are you looking for a sales associate? I have experience.
I am excited to apply for the Sales Associate position at SportChek, and I am confident my customer service skills make me a great fit.
Hello, I want to work at your store.
To Whom It May Concern, I am applying for a job.

questions.stem: Revise the following opening to make it professional and effective: 'Are you hiring? I think I could work at your company.'
questions.rubric: The opening must state a specific job title, express genuine enthusiasm, and not begin with a question. For example: 'I am writing to apply for the [Job Title] position at [Company Name], and I am eager to bring my skills to your team.'

retestCards.passRule: Must answer both questions correctly: select the correct option for question 1, and provide a revised opening that includes a job title, enthusiasm, and no question for question 2.

questions.stem: Which of the following closing paragraphs includes a proper call to action for an interview?
options: Thank you for your time. I hope to hear from you soon.
Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss my qualifications further in an interview.
I am excited about this job. Please let me know if you need more information.

questions.stem: Imagine you are applying for a position as a customer service representative at a local bank. Write a closing paragraph for your cover letter that includes both a thank-you and a confident call to action for an interview.
questions.rubric: Must include an expression of thanks and a direct request for an interview (e.g., 'I look forward to discussing my qualifications in an interview').

retestCards.passRule: Must answer the multiple choice correctly and the open-ended response must include both a thank-you and a call to action for an interview.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the purpose of a cover letter compared to a resume?
options: A cover letter repeats your resume in paragraph form.
A cover letter tells a story connecting your skills to the employer’s needs.
A cover letter is a short version of your resume.

questions.stem: You are applying for a customer service representative job. Rewrite the following experience to connect it to the job: 'I was a cashier at a school bake sale.'
questions.rubric: Answer should show translation: e.g., 'As a cashier at a school bake sale, I handled transactions, provided friendly service, and managed money, skills directly applicable to a customer service role.' Must link the experience to at least one job-relevant skill (e.g., customer service, cash handling, communication).

retestCards.passRule: Correct answer on single-choice (index 1) and open-ended response that demonstrates experience translation (linking bake sale cashier role to customer service skills).

questions.stem: Why do employers typically require cover letters to be submitted as PDF rather than Word (.docx)?
options: PDF files are smaller in size and easier to email.
PDF preserves formatting (fonts, spacing, layout) across different computers and operating systems.
PDF is the only format that can include digital signatures.
PDF files cannot contain viruses, making them safer for employers.

questions.stem: Explain two potential problems with submitting a cover letter in Word (.docx) format and how saving as a PDF solves each issue.
questions.rubric: Student must identify two distinct problems. Acceptable problems include: (1) Word documents may display differently (fonts change, spacing shifts) on the employer's computer, making it look unprofessional; PDF locks the layout so it appears exactly as intended. (2) Word documents are easily editable, which could lead to accidental changes or ethical concerns; PDF is read-only, preserving the original content. Each problem should be paired with a clear explanation of how PDF resolves it. Partial credit for one fully explained problem.

retestCards.passRule: Must select correct option for single choice question AND provide at least one valid problem-solution pair in open-ended response.

dashboardFormat.objective: Cover letters are a professional story connecting applicant skills to employer needs, distinct from resumes which list work/education history.；Canadian cover letters require 1-inch margins, professional fonts (Arial/Times New Roman/Calibri) 10-12pt, single spacing with double spacing between paragraphs, left-aligned.；Header includes: full name, street address, phone, professional email, full written date, hiring manager name/title/company/address.

learningGoals.statement: Identify the purpose of a cover letter and differentiate it from a resume.
Apply correct formatting, header, salutation, opening, and closing rules for a Canadian cover letter.
Translate personal experiences into workplace skills relevant to the job posting.
Follow manual proofreading and PDF submission requirements.

courseOpsItems.title: Academic Integrity: No AI/Translation Use
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Ensure all submissions are original; avoid using AI or translation tools.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: Keth Kinsey explicitly states that submitting AI-generated or machine-translated work is a far worse outcome than submitting no assignment at all.

courseOpsItems.title: Interview Recording: Unplanned Questions
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Ensure interview recording contains at least 3 on-the-spot follow-up questions.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: Mandatory unplanned questions: All students must include at least 3 unplanned, on-the-spot follow-up questions in their interview recordings.

courseOpsItems.title: Job Posting Research
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Find a real English-language entry-level job posting (e.g., on Indeed), take a screenshot, and submit.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: Job posting research: Locate a real, English-language entry-level job posting from a platform such as Indeed, take a clear screenshot of the full posting for formal submission.

courseOpsItems.title: Cover Letter Graphic Organizer
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Complete all 7 fields of the graphic organizer from Schoology Unit 2 Lesson 15 shared folder.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: Fill out all 7 required fields of the cover letter graphic organizer posted to the Schoology Unit 2 Lesson 15 shared folder.

courseOpsItems.title: Cover Letter Draft Submission
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Write a 1-page (under 300 words) cover letter following the high-quality model, manually proofread, and submit all materials to Schoology assignment dropbox.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: Cover letter drafting and submission: Write a 1-page (under 300 word) cover letter following the provided high-quality model, proofread manually, and submit all three materials to the Schoology assignment dropbox.

courseOpsItems.title: No AI Proofreading Tools
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Do not use Grammarly or other AI proofreading tools; proofread manually 2-3 times.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: Manual proofreading mandate: Manually proofread the full document at least 2 to 3 times to catch spelling and grammar errors, as AI proofreading tools like Grammarly are prohibited for this assignment.

courseOpsUncertainItems.rawText: Unspecified deadline for follow-up work (job posting research, graphic organizer, cover letter draft)
courseOpsUncertainItems.reason: No explicit due date mentioned; likely due next class but not confirmed.

courseOpsUncertainItems.rawText: Interview recording requirement (unplanned questions) unclear whether for past or future assignment
courseOpsUncertainItems.reason: Context suggests it's for the narrative assignment, but timing not specified.

cards.question: Which statement best describes the main purpose of a cover letter?
options: To list all of your work and education history in paragraph form.
To introduce yourself and request an interview politely.
To connect your skills and experiences to the specific employer's needs in a professional story.
To show off your vocabulary and writing style.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands the unique role of a cover letter vs. a resume.
misconceptions: That is the purpose of a resume, not a cover letter. A cover letter tells a targeted story.
While polite, this is too vague. A cover letter specifically connects your skills to the employer's needs.
✓ Correct! A cover letter is a narrative that shows why you are a great fit for the job.
Writing style matters, but the core purpose is to match your skills to the job, not to impress with language.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies that a cover letter is a targeted narrative connecting applicant skills to employer needs, not a repeat of the resume.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces ...

cards.commonMisconception: Students think cover letters simply repeat resume content or serve as a formal introduction.

cards.question: Which salutation is most appropriate for a cover letter when you do not know the hiring manager's name?
options: To Whom It May Concern,
Hello,
Dear Sir/Madam,
To the Retail Manager Hiring Team at SportChek,
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows to avoid 'To Whom It May Concern' or 'Hello' and use a role-based salutation.
misconceptions: Too generic. Try to address the specific role or department.
Too casual for a formal cover letter. Always use a professional salutation.
Outdated and generic. Use a more specific alternative.
✓ Correct! This salutation is specific and professional.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects a specific, professional salutation rather than casual or generic ones.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces ...
cards.alignmentNote: Question tests conventions of a cover letter (salutation), a specific writing form under B2.
cards.commonMisconception: Students default to 'To Whom It May Concern' or casual 'Hello'.

cards.question: Which sentence from a cover letter opening paragraph would be most effective?
options: Are you looking for a hardworking employee?
I am writing to apply for the Sales Associate position at your downtown location, and I am excited about the opportunity to contribute to your team.
I think I would be great for this job because I have experience.
You probably receive many applications, but mine is special.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student avoids opening with a question and instead states the job and enthusiasm.
misconceptions: Never open with a question. It signals you haven't researched the company.

Too vague. Specify the job title and show enthusiasm.

A list of all my skills again.
A question about the hiring timeline.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student recalls the call-to-action requirement.
misconceptions: A thank-you is good, but you also need a confident call to action requesting an interview.

The closing is not for repeating skills; it's for a call to action.
Avoid questions in the closing. State your request for an interview.
cards.successCriteria: Student knows that a confident call to action for an interview is required.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces ...

cards.commonMisconception: Students think only thanking is sufficient, or they omit the interview request.

cards.diagnosis: Check if student connects extracurricular to workplace skills rather than merely listing the activity.

Too vague and not connected to the job.
Personal preferences are not professional skills. Focus on transferable skills.
cards.successCriteria: Student chooses to translate the experience into relevant workplace skills rather than just listing it.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces ...

cards.question: A student is writing a cover letter for a retail position. Which experience would be BEST to include in the body?
options: My hobby of playing video games for five hours a day.
Organizing a school bake sale where I managed cash and interacted with customers.
I enjoy watching movies and reading books.
I participated in a school talent show.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can judge relevance of experiences to the target job.
misconceptions: Unless directly relevant (e.g., applying at a gaming store), this is irrelevant and unprofessional.
✓ Correct! This translates to cash handling and customer service, which are directly relevant to retail.
Too general and not clearly transferable to retail skills.
This could show confidence, but it's less directly linked to retail skills than the bake sale experience.
cards.successCriteria: Student selects an experience that can be translated into retail-relevant skills, avoiding irrelevant hobbies.
cards.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces ...
cards.alignmentNote: Requires evaluating which experiences are job-relevant, a key skill for B2 writing.
cards.commonMisconception: Students include hobbies like video gaming that have no connection to the job.
